The faith, thought through.

Long-form articles on Christian doctrine: what the church actually confesses, where the words came from, and — just as carefully — what the explanations cannot do. Every quotation is from a named edition, and every analogy comes with the limit its own author set on it.

Parts, each read on its own
Passages quoted in full
Sources, each with its edition
One doctrine at a time. Taken slowly.

Each article sets out a question, answers it from Scripture and the primary sources, and says plainly where the answer stops. They are long on purpose: these are subjects that go wrong when they are made short.
The Trinity one God, three persons
What does the church actually confess about the Trinity — and why does every explanation of it break?

The confession, in the words the creeds use. Why ice, water and steam and the man with three jobs are both the same third-century error. The analogies Augustine, Aquinas, the Cappadocians and C. S. Lewis did offer, each one placed beside the limit its own author wrote for it. And the two councils, fifty-six years apart, that drew the fences.
What the Trinity is One God. Three persons.
Why the usual pictures fail Ice, water, steam — and a man with three jobs.
The analogies of the great theologians Every picture came with its own warning.
Where the words came from Nicaea 325, Constantinople 381.
Four rules, kept throughout.
Primary sources, quoted and located
When Augustine or Aquinas or a council is quoted, the words are theirs, the translation is named, and the reference is exact enough to look up. Nothing is paraphrased and then put in quotation marks.
Scripture in modern English
All Bible quotations are the Berean Standard Bible, given to the public domain in 2023, and each one links to the same wording in this site’s reader.
Every analogy with its limit attached
An illustration is allowed to make one point. Wherever an article offers one, it also says, in the same place, what the picture cannot carry — usually in the words of the person who drew it.
Work still in copyright is described, not reproduced

Where a modern author’s argument matters, it is summarised in our own words and labelled as ours, with the book and chapter to read it in. The quotations on this site are from editions that are free for anyone to copy.
Named editions. Nothing taken on trust.

Every source quoted anywhere in this section, with its translator, its edition and its licence. Where this site holds the text, the link opens our copy; otherwise it opens the edition the words were read in.
